who: Peter W. Topping, historian of medieval and later Greece, University of Cincinnati, PhD Pennsylvania 1942.

evidence.says: The archive identifies Peter W. Topping, PhD in medieval history at Pennsylvania in 1942, and professor of History and Later Greek Studies at Cincinnati, 1961–1978.
Authority heading is Topping, Peter W.; cites the American School of Classical Studies and Feudal institutions as revealed in the Assizes of Romania (1949).

notes: Exact doctorate and relevant Cincinnati appointment identify this candidate. The documented appointment covers the 1973 dissertation; the 1980 and 1986 completions postdate it.

who: Robert D. Warth, historian of Russia and the Soviet Union, University of Kentucky.

evidence.says: A June 1977 review of The Secret Police in Lenin’s Russia names Robert D. Warth with University of Kentucky affiliation.
Identifies Robert D. Warth as professor emeritus of history at Kentucky and author of Nicholas II.
Authority heading is Warth, Robert D.; cites The Allies and the Russian Revolution (1954).

notes: Name, Russian-history specialization and Kentucky affiliation during the listed supervision period agree. The Chicago doctorate year was not independently confirmed.

who: Lee Windsor, military historian at the University of New Brunswick, PhD UNB 2006.

evidence.says: UNB identifies Windsor as an associate professor who teaches and supervises modern warfare, with a UNB PhD; lists Kandahar Tour among his publications.
In 2014 Windsor was UNB Gregg Centre deputy director and Eaton Chair in Canadian Army Studies, with a UNB PhD.
The book listing for Steel Cavalry identifies its author Lee Windsor as PhD ’06 and UNB Gregg Centre deputy director.
This Lee Windsor authority is established from Kandahar tour (2008), the same work listed on his faculty profile.

notes: Publication identity, institution and doctorate agree. The other Lee Windsor authority concerns On website development (2018).

who: Judith Schachter [Modell], professor of anthropology and history at Carnegie Mellon, PhD Minnesota 1978.

evidence.says: CMU identifies Judith Schachter [Modell] as professor emerita of anthropology and history, department member since 1984, with a Minnesota PhD in 1978.
The authority links Judith Schachter and Judith Schachter Modell, author of Ruth Benedict: Patterns of a Life; its CMU citation identifies her as anthropology and history professor there since 1984.

notes: Authority record explicitly identifies the CMU faculty member, and the Minnesota doctorate agrees. Judith Claire Schachter is a separate Oxford international-relations thesis author.

who: Paul Létourneau, historian of modern Germany and international relations, Université de Montréal, doctorate Strasbourg.

evidence.says: The 2012 degree list names Paul Létourneau as research director for Frédéric Cyr’s PhD in history, Rebelle devant les extrêmes: Paul Levi, une biographie politique.
Lists Paul Létourneau as full professor, doctorate Strasbourg, specializing in modern German history and twentieth-century international relations.
Paul Létourneau’s article on Rathenau identifies him as professor in the Université de Montréal history department.
Authority for Létourneau, Paul cites his Walther Rathenau (1987), whose cover identifies an international-relations teacher at the Collège militaire royal de Saint-Jean since 1981.

notes: Direct supervision evidence establishes the Montréal historian; the candidate’s name, Rathenau scholarship and international-relations field agree.

who: Robert I. Crane, historian of South Asia at Syracuse University.

evidence.says: A 1969–1970 visitor list identifies Dr. Robert I. Crane as director of the South Asia Program at Syracuse University.
Syracuse’s repository records Robert I. Crane as author of Problems in Development of Nationalism in India (1986).
The 1991 volume The Congress and Indian Nationalism lists Robert I. Crane with Syracuse University affiliation.
Authority heading is Crane, Robert I.; cites Aspects of economic development in South Asia (1954) and records a PhD.

notes: The Syracuse South Asia scholar matches the candidate’s full name and subject, in the relevant period. The individual student-advisor relationships were not independently reverified.

who: Bingham Duncan, historian of American diplomacy and commerce at Emory University.

evidence.says: The 1956 contributor note identifies Bingham Duncan as associate professor of history at Emory, researching late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century American diplomacy and commerce.
Authority heading is Duncan, Bingham, established from Whitelaw Reid (1975).
The 1976 scholarly review identifies Bingham Duncan as author of Whitelaw Reid: Journalist, Politician, Diplomat (University of Georgia Press, 1975).

notes: The distinctive name, Emory appointment and American diplomatic-history work agree with the supervision record. Later individual supervision dates were not independently confirmed.

who: Randolph E. Bergstrom, historian of American social policy and public history at UC Santa Barbara, PhD Columbia.

evidence.says: The UCSB history faculty list identifies Randolph Bergstrom, PhD Columbia, with American social policy and public history specializations.
The department newsletter announces Randolph Bergstrom joining UCSB and describes his Columbia dissertation, Courting Danger: The Evolution of Tort Liability in New York, 1870–1910.
Authority heading is Bergstrom, Randolph E. (Randolph Emil); cites Courting danger (1992).
Identifies Randolph E. Bergstrom as author of Courting Danger: Injury and Law in New York City, 1870–1910 (1992).

notes: UCSB affiliation, Columbia doctorate and the distinctive Courting Danger research establish the match to n92039771.
